Where we measured

Coverage

all sessions, regardless of the filters above
Target areaPhase-1 areaStartedTarget metEqual-area hexagons of about 610,000 km² (H3 level 1) with at least 100,000 inhabitants

The world is divided into equal-area hexagons of about 610,000 km² (H3 level 1), independent of borders; the 297 with at least 100,000 inhabitants are target areas. Each area needs at least 1 place (a city, town or village); populous areas need more, in proportion to the square root of their population (at most 8). Each place needs 4 sessions, one per site type (station or plaza; shopping or mixed-use street; residential; park). Phase 1 consists of the partner areas (Netherlands, Switzerland, Colorado, Alabama and Cape Town) plus a spread-out subset of other areas that do not touch each other or a partner area. Urbanisation is estimated from each session's coordinates: City = within the estimated core (1,500 inhabitants per km²) of a place with at least 50,000 inhabitants; Town = within the estimated area (300 per km²) of a place with at least 5,000 inhabitants; otherwise Rural. Region names for large countries from ISO 3166-2. Populations are approximate, from GeoNames (CC BY 4.0).

Differences by sex and age

Women vs men

Age groups

Sex difference within each age group

Mean ± SD per group. Differences come with a confidence interval (Welch) and effect size d (difference ÷ pooled SD); a difference in bold has an interval that excludes zero. The three age comparisons use 98.3% intervals (Bonferroni for three comparisons). Only trials with one age group are used for age. Groups are not adjusted for each other or for location, so read these as descriptive differences.

Normalised to estimated body height

Body height is not measured. Each trial gets the mean height for its country, sex and age group from NCD-RisC (2016). This corrects group averages for height differences between countries and between men and women, not individual people. Read it next to the raw values.

Dotted lines in these three charts follow speed = cadence ÷ 60 × step length, so each one marks a constant value of the quantity that is not on the axes.

Step-time asymmetry

bins of 2 %

Asymmetry compares the time of left and right steps, using the order of the heel-strike taps. Observers tap by eye, so small asymmetries fall within tapping error; values above about 10 % are the ones to look at.

Definitions. Speed = distance between the marks ÷ time from Start to Stop. Cadence = steps per minute between the first and last heel strike. Step length = speed ÷ step frequency. Valid trials exclude trials marked as error, trials out of the plausible walking range (speed 0.4–2.5 m/s, cadence 60–160 steps/min, step length 0.3–1.2 m) and walking backwards, unless you include them above. Each trial records the version of the Global Gait tool that collected it; the version is listed per session and in the CSV.

Country comes from the site's coordinates; when those are missing it uses the country the researcher typed.

Height normalisation. Estimated height = NCD-RisC (2016) mean adult height for the trial's country and sex, averaged over the birth years of its age group (reference year 2026; the data end at birth year 1996, and height loss in old age is not included). Leg length = 0.53 × height. Froude speed = speed ÷ √(9.81 × leg length). Step length ÷ height uses the same estimate. The CSV also gives dimensionless cadence = step frequency × √(leg length ÷ 9.81) (Hof 1996). Source: NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, eLife 2016;5:e13410.
